summary: Hearth - Hear Earth turns NASA Earth data into sound, so the state of the planet can be heard as well as seen, and the whole app can be used without sight. It is an Earth Information Jukebox of thirteen scenes. Six are about Earth: the planet itself, tuned to its Schumann resonance; global temperature from NASA GISTEMP (1880–2025); Arctic sea ice (1979–2025); Mauna Loa CO₂, where you hear the planet breathe each year (1958–2026); rising seas (1880–2023); and an Earth Information Center that reads NASA imagery, including live layers from NASA GIBS, as sound. Seven more cover the sky, from an aurora driven by live NOAA space-weather data to the Moon, Sun, stars, Halley’s comet and the asteroid Eros. Every scene has spoken narration, live data readouts with their sources, a legend that explains each sound, a 60-second audio export, and a 3D picture driven by the same data. No number is typed in by hand, and tests check every claim the narration makes against the data.
details:
What it does
Hearth is an Earth Information Jukebox: thirteen scenes that turn NASA Earth and sky data into sound, designed so that someone who cannot see the screen still gets the whole story. Each scene plays its data as sound, narrates what you are hearing, reads out the values and where they came from, and draws a 3D picture driven by the same state as the sound. You choose scenes with the number keys.

How it works
Each dataset is mapped to sound in a way you can learn by ear. In The breathing planet, pitch follows the monthly Mauna Loa CO₂ concentration at one octave per 60 ppm. Each year’s seasonal swing is a sigh of about a semitone, while the long rise climbs nearly two octaves. In Rising seas, each wave is a year of water arriving and the pitch is the height of the sea. Aurora takes the real emission lines of oxygen and nitrogen and lowers them forty octaves into audible notes. Its intensity follows the live NOAA planetary K index when that can be reached, and a simulated storm otherwise. The comet’s pulse rate comes from its orbital speed, solved from Halley’s real orbital elements. The Earth Information Center reads whole-Earth images through lenses for night lights, ocean, lightning, carbon and forest. Two images are built in from NASA (Blue Marble and Earth at Night 2012), and 14 more layers are fetched live from NASA GIBS. You can also explore a frame by arrow keys or touch, or drop in your own image or video.

Accessibility
Every scene has narration, spoken data with sources, and a legend that plays each sound alongside its meaning. Preferences cover voice, auto-narration, binaural placement, screen-reader announcements, captions, reduced motion, theme, haptics, and a choice of 3D, ring or no picture. Any scene can be saved as a 60-second WAV file.

Data you can check
No numbers are typed in by hand. A build script generates the app’s data from source snapshots and records each file’s source, URL and checksum. Forty unit tests check the sound mappings, the data parsers, and every factual claim the narration makes against the data. If a live source can’t be reached, the app says so and falls back gracefully.

Why it matters
Climate data is usually shown as charts, which shuts out people who are blind or have low vision, as well as many people who don’t read graphs easily. Hearing the planet breathe, or the sea rising faster each decade, makes long-term change something you can grasp in seconds.

Tools
JavaScript, the Web Audio API, WebGL through Three.js, and Node.js for the build scripts and tests. It runs in any modern browser, either hosted on GitHub Pages or as a single HTML file. The code is at https://github.com/TheBestProEver/experience
